extracted.intended_audience: environmental lawyers, administrative-law practitioners, agency officials, judges, and litigants challenging or defending EPA rulemaking decisions
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria for litigating and reviewing EPA denials of rulemaking petitions under the Clean Air Act and the Administrative Procedure Act, including standing, statutory interpretation, and arbitrary-and-capricious review. Focuses on whether greenhouse gases are 'air pollutants' and what constitutes a reasoned agency judgment to regulate or decline to regulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article III standing elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To demonstrate standing a litigant must show a concrete and particularized injury that is actual or imminent, that the injury is fairly traceable to the defendant, and that a favorable decision will likely redress that injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife; explains that these three elements (injury-in-fact, causation, redressability) are required in ordinary cases. Notes that only one petitioner needs standing to authorize review (cites Rumsfeld v. FAIR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional procedural-rights can relax redressability/immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A litigant to whom Congress has accorded a procedural right to protect his concrete interests can assert that right without meeting all normal standards for redressability and immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Lujan, noting the special rule applies where Congress has provided a procedural right (here, the right to challenge agency action unlawfully withheld under §7607(b)(1)). This allows standing even if normal redressability or immediacy tests are not fully satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: State sovereign standing considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: A State has a special position and interest for standing: as sovereign, owning territory, and possessing prerogatives to protect its citizens and resources, which can establish injury and redressability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains Massachusetts' sovereign interests (land threatened by sea-level rise, prerogatives such as negotiating treaties or exercising police powers) and that Congress ordered EPA to protect states via §7521(a)(1), giving states a concomitant procedural right under §7607(b)(1). The holdings emphasize that state-specific harms can satisfy the 'most demanding standards' of adversarial process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of harm from climate change as injury
rubrics_metrics.description: Harms associated with climate change are serious and well recognized and can constitute injury-in-fact (e.g., sea-level rise, irreversible ecosystem changes, loss of snowpack, disease spread, more severe weather).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court relies on uncontested affidavits and scientific consensus, stating sea-level rise and remediation costs as concrete examples. The ubiquity of the harms does not diminish a state's interest (cites Federal Election Comm'n v. Akins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation/traceability in climate-change cases
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's refusal to regulate that contributes to greenhouse-gas emissions can be fairly traced to petitioners' injuries; marginal domestic contributions need not be globally decisive to satisfy causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects EPA's argument that foreign emissions offset any domestic regulation; explains agencies and legislatures work incrementally and a first step need not solve the entire problem. Domestic regulation that 'contributes' to mitigation suffices for traceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redressability in incremental/multijurisdictional problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A remedy that would slow or reduce harm, even if not reverse it or if its benefits are delayed, can satisfy redressability for standing purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court says delay until vehicle fleet turns over is irrelevant and that slowing the pace of global emissions by domestic action still meaningfully affects harms, so redressability is not defeated because other countries may increase emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewability of denials of rulemaking petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Denials of rulemaking petitions that are expressly made reviewable by statute (here §7607(b)(1)) are subject to judicial review and are different from ordinary nonenforcement decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes Heckler v. Chaney (nonenforcement usually unreviewable) from denials of rulemaking petitions where Congress granted review; thus courts may review such denials on the merits under the statutory standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for EPA action under Clean Air Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §7607(d)(9), courts may reverse agency action if it is arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court frames its ability to reverse the EPA's denial under the Administrative Procedure Act/CAA standard and will assess whether EPA's stated reasons are grounded in the statute and supported by reasoned explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of 'air pollutant' encompasses greenhouse gases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act defines 'air pollutant' to include 'any air pollution agent … , including any physical, chemical … substance … emitted into … the ambient air,' a capacious definition that embraces greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court emphasizes the repeated 'any' in the statutory text and states greenhouse gases are 'physical [and] chemical … substance[s].' Rejects EPA's contrary interpretation based on post-enactment events.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA has statutory authority to regulate greenhouse gases from new motor vehicles
rubrics_metrics.description: Because greenhouse gases fall within the Clean Air Act's definition of 'air pollutant', EPA has authority under §7521(a)(1) to regulate emissions from new motor vehicles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court rejects EPA reliance on subsequent congressional actions or policy overlaps (e.g., DOT mileage standards) as a reason to shirk statutory duty; overlap with DOT does not license EPA to avoid protecting health and welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper scope of EPA's 'judgment' under §7521(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's judgment must relate to whether an air pollutant 'cause[s], or contribute[s] to, air pollution which may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If EPA concludes it does not contribute, or provides a reasonable explanation why it cannot form that judgment, it may refrain from regulation. But the judgment must be grounded in the statutory question about contribution to endangerment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited bases for declining to regulate under the statute
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may not decline to regulate based on policy considerations unrelated to whether the pollutant contributes to endangerment, such as reliance on voluntary Executive Branch programs or concern about impairing presidential negotiations with other nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court finds EPA's 'laundry list' of policy reasons insufficient and says such considerations are 'divorced from the statutory text.' These are impermissible reasons for denying rulemaking under §7607(d)(9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific uncertainty and reasoned explanation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If scientific uncertainty is so profound that it precludes a reasoned judgment, the agency must explicitly say so; otherwise, uncertainty alone is not a permissible justification for declining to make an endangerment finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must explain whether sufficient information exists for an endangerment finding; it cannot simply cite uncertainty without providing a reasoned explanation that shows why it cannot form the necessary judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to ground actions or inaction in statutory terms on remand
rubrics_metrics.description: On remand the agency must ground its reasons for action or inaction in the statute and provide a reasoned explanation consistent with the governing legal standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court directs EPA to base its future decisions on statutory predicates and to avoid impermissible policy justifications, effectively instructing the agency what a lawful record and rationale must address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incrementalism and agency decisionmaking legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's choice to address a massive problem incrementally does not negate federal-court jurisdiction or render an initial regulatory action impermissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court analogizes to legislative incrementalism (Williamson v. Lee Optical) and agency refinement over time (SEC v. Chenery), explaining that tentative first steps are lawful and do not defeat standing or reviewability.
